report:
## Conclusion: The evidence does not support that ivermectin lowers the risk of death in COVID-19

While some early, smaller meta-analyses suggested a mortality benefit, the totality of high-quality evidence now points the other way.

**Evidence against a benefit:**
- A **JAMA meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials** found that favorable mortality results were limited to trials in regions with high prevalence of strongyloidiasis (a parasitic infection ivermectin treats), with no mortality benefit in low-prevalence regions — suggesting any apparent effect may reflect parasite co-infection rather than antiviral action. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/ivermectin-for-covid)
- The large **ACTIV-6 / NEJM trial** (1,800 outpatients) found ivermectin did not significantly reduce hospitalization or prolonged emergency observation compared with placebo. (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869)
- The **PRINCIPLE trial** (Oxford, 2024) concluded ivermectin "does not provide clinically meaningful" benefits in recovery time, hospitalization, or mortality. (https://www.principletrial.org/news/new-study-shows-ivermectin-lacks-meaningful-benefits-in-covid-19-treatment)
- In **November 2023, WHO updated its guidelines to recommend strongly against** ivermectin for COVID-19, citing lack of evidence and biological plausibility. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic)

**Evidence cited for benefit** came mostly from early, small, or lower-quality trials, some later retracted for flawed or fabricated data. When meta-analyses prioritized trial quality and excluded suspect data, the apparent mortality benefit disappeared.

**Bottom line:** Your view ("yes") reflects early signals that have not been confirmed by large, well-conducted randomized trials or by WHO and major guideline bodies. The current best evidence indicates ivermectin does **not** meaningfully reduce COVID-19 mortality.
